guideTitle: The Best Docking Stations for MacBook Air, Matched to Your Chip
metaTitle: Best Docking Stations for MacBook Air: Single, Dual and Triple Displays (2026)
metaDescription: We compared MacBook Air docks by how they drive external displays, Thunderbolt or DisplayLink, and by charging, ports and Ethernet, with notes on what each Air chip supports.
introParagraphs: With a MacBook Air, the chip decides more than the dock. M1 and M2 Airs support one external display natively. The M3 Air supports two only with the lid closed, and the M4 Air supports two with the lid open. A dock cannot change that, unless it uses DisplayLink, which sends extra displays through software and a driver.

That makes the first question how many monitors you want. For one monitor, a simple USB-C hub is enough. For two or three on an older Air, you need a DisplayLink dock, with its trade-offs: a driver to install, some processor load, and output that is less suited to color-critical work. Hubs that list dual HDMI without DisplayLink generally show the same image on both screens on macOS.
Our comparison is based on published specifications, Apple's published display support and price position, not hands-on testing. Prices range from about $40 to $200 at the time of writing.

plugable-tbt-udm-thunderbolt-4.badge: Best Thunderbolt Dock for M4 and Newer
plugable-tbt-udm-thunderbolt-4.summary: A Thunderbolt 4-certified dock with 100W charging, six USB ports, SD and Ethernet.
plugable-tbt-udm-thunderbolt-4.description:
The Plugable TBT-UDM is the dock for a newer Air that can drive displays natively: a Thunderbolt 4-certified dock that Plugable lists for M4 and M5 MacBooks, supporting two 4K HDMI monitors or a single 6K display without drivers.

It adds 100W charging, which is far more than an Air needs but leaves headroom for other devices, plus six USB ports, an SD slot and Ethernet.

On an M1 or M2 Air it will still drive only one external display, and it costs about $200 at the time of writing.
specs: Displays: 2 x 4K HDMI or 1 x 6K (on supported Macs)
cons: Only one external display on M1/M2 Airs
plugable-tbt-udm-thunderbolt-4.bestFor: M4 or newer Air owners who want native dual displays and a full desk dock.
plugable-tbt-udm-thunderbolt-4.skipIf: You have an M1 or M2 Air and want two monitors; you need a DisplayLink dock.

tobenone-18-in-2-macbook-dock.badge: Best DisplayLink Dock for Dual Monitors
tobenone-18-in-2-macbook-dock.summary: A DisplayLink dock for two 4K 60Hz displays, with a 150W adapter and 2.5G Ethernet.
tobenone-18-in-2-macbook-dock.description:
The TobenONE 18-in-2 is the pick for M1, M2 or M3 Air owners who want two monitors with the lid open: it uses DisplayLink to add a second 4K 60Hz display beyond the chip's native limit.

It includes a 150W power adapter, 2.5G Ethernet, 10Gbps USB-C, seven USB ports and an SD 4.0 reader, which makes it a full desk hub.

DisplayLink needs a driver, adds some processor load, and is less suited to color-critical editing. It is bulkier than a single-cable hub.
tobenone-18-in-2-macbook-dock.bestFor: M1–M3 Air owners who need two monitors with the lid open.
tobenone-18-in-2-macbook-dock.skipIf: You have an M4 or newer Air; a Thunderbolt dock drives two displays natively.

pulwtop-dual-monitor-dock.summary: Dual HDMI at 4K 60Hz via DisplayLink, with Ethernet and a card reader, for about $70.
pulwtop-dual-monitor-dock.description:
The PULWTOP is the budget route to two monitors on an older Air: dual HDMI outputs at 4K 60Hz via DisplayLink, for about $70 at the time of writing.

It adds 10Gbps USB-A and USB-C, an SD/TF slot, Ethernet and power pass-through.

It has fewer ports than the TobenONE docks, a plastic build, and the usual DisplayLink trade-offs.
pulwtop-dual-monitor-dock.bestFor: Budget buyers with an M1–M3 Air who need two monitors.
pulwtop-dual-monitor-dock.skipIf: You want 2.5G Ethernet and more ports; the TobenONE 18-in-2 has them.

tobenone-17-in-2-macbook-dock.summary: A DisplayLink dual-4K dock listed for M1 to M5 Macs, with a 150W charger and 2.5G Ethernet.
tobenone-17-in-2-macbook-dock.description:
The TobenONE 17-in-2 is a close sibling of the 18-in-2, listed for Macs from M1 to M5, which suits a shared desk where different MacBooks connect.

It includes a 150W charger, seven USB ports at up to 10Gbps and 2.5G Ethernet, with dual 4K displays via DisplayLink.

It costs about $10 more than the 18-in-2 at the time of writing and is close in price to the Thunderbolt Plugable. The DisplayLink trade-offs apply.
tobenone-17-in-2-macbook-dock.bestFor: Desks shared by several MacBooks of different generations.
tobenone-17-in-2-macbook-dock.skipIf: Only one Mac uses the desk; the 18-in-2 is similar for less.

anker-dl6350-triple-display.summary: A DisplayLink dock for three displays, with dual HDMI and DisplayPort.
anker-dl6350-triple-display.description:
The Anker DL6350 is the only dock here for three external monitors, which no MacBook Air can drive natively; it does this through DisplayLink.

It offers two HDMI outputs and a DisplayPort, 10 ports in total, and works with Windows as well as macOS. Anker is an established name for DisplayLink docks.

It is the most expensive dock here at the time of writing, three DisplayLink displays add more processor load, and the output is not ideal for color-critical work.
anker-dl6350-triple-display.bestFor: Air owners who need three monitors.
anker-dl6350-triple-display.skipIf: Two monitors are enough; the TobenONE or PULWTOP cost less.

anker-8-in-1-dual-monitor-dock.summary: An 8-in-1 hub with dual HDMI, 85W pass-through, Ethernet and SD; charger not included.
anker-8-in-1-dual-monitor-dock.description:
The Anker 8-in-1 is an inexpensive hub with two HDMI outputs, 85W power pass-through, gigabit Ethernet and an SD reader, for about $54 at the time of writing.

The listing does not state that it uses DisplayLink. Without DisplayLink, a MacBook Air generally cannot show different content on two monitors through a hub like this, so on macOS treat it as a one-monitor hub unless Anker confirms otherwise.

The power adapter is sold separately.
cons: Dual extended displays on a Mac not confirmed
anker-8-in-1-dual-monitor-dock.bestFor: Air owners who want one monitor plus Ethernet and SD.
anker-8-in-1-dual-monitor-dock.skipIf: You need two separate monitors; choose a DisplayLink dock.

wavlink-13-in-1-displaylink-dock.summary: A DisplayLink dock for two displays up to 5K, with HDMI and DisplayPort and 130W charging.
wavlink-13-in-1-displaylink-dock.description:
The WAVLINK 13-in-1 is the DisplayLink dock for sharper monitors: it lists dual displays up to 5K, with two HDMI and two DisplayPort outputs so you can match your monitors' inputs.

It adds 130W power delivery, five USB ports and audio, and is listed for M1 to M4 Macs and Windows.

DisplayLink trade-offs apply, and it costs more than the budget dual-display docks.
wavlink-13-in-1-displaylink-dock.bestFor: Air owners with higher-resolution monitors who need two displays.
wavlink-13-in-1-displaylink-dock.skipIf: Your monitors are 4K or lower; the TobenONE or PULWTOP cost less.

ugreen-revodok-pro-210.badge: Best Compact Hub for One Monitor
ugreen-revodok-pro-210.summary: A compact 10-in-1 USB-C hub with 100W pass-through, Ethernet and a card reader for about $40.
ugreen-revodok-pro-210.description:
The UGREEN Revodok Pro 210 is the small, inexpensive choice for a single external monitor: a 10-in-1 USB-C hub with HDMI, 100W power pass-through, 5Gbps data, gigabit Ethernet and an SD/TF reader.

It is easy to carry and suits travel or a minimal desk.

UGREEN lists dual HDMI, but it is a USB-C hub rather than a DisplayLink or Thunderbolt dock, so on a MacBook Air expect one extended display; a second screen will generally mirror the first.
specs: Display: HDMI up to 4K 60Hz (one extended display on Macs)
cons: One extended display on a Mac
ugreen-revodok-pro-210.skipIf: You need two monitors; choose a DisplayLink dock.

buyingCriteria.explanation: M1 and M2: one external display. M3: two with the lid closed. M4: two with the lid open. More than that requires DisplayLink.

DisplayLink docks (TobenONE, PULWTOP, Anker DL6350, WAVLINK) add displays via a driver, with some processor load and less color accuracy. Thunderbolt and USB-C hubs drive displays natively, within your chip's limit.
macOS generally mirrors rather than extends across two outputs on a basic USB-C hub. Do not rely on a hub's dual HDMI for two separate screens unless it uses DisplayLink.
An Air needs far less than 100W; extra wattage helps charge other devices. Some hubs need your own charger; the TobenONE docks include one.
2.5G Ethernet (TobenONE) only helps on a faster network. Check card reader and USB speed if you move large files.

faq.q: Can any dock give my MacBook Air two external displays?
faq.a: On an M1 or M2 Air, only a DisplayLink dock can. An M3 Air supports two natively with the lid closed, and an M4 Air with the lid open.

faq.q: Do I need a 100W dock for a MacBook Air?
faq.a: No. The Air draws much less. Extra wattage only helps if you charge other devices through the dock.

faq.q: Why does my Air slow down when docked?
faq.a: The Air has no fan, so heavy sustained loads, including driving several DisplayLink displays, can lead it to reduce performance to manage heat. Reducing the number of displays may help.

faq.q: Is a Thunderbolt dock better than a USB-C hub?
faq.a: For one monitor and basic ports, a hub is enough. A Thunderbolt dock offers more bandwidth and, on M4 or newer Airs, native dual displays.

faq.q: Can I charge through MagSafe while docked?
faq.a: Yes. Using MagSafe for power leaves the USB-C port connected to the dock for data and display.

bottomLine: Start with your chip. For one monitor, the UGREEN Revodok Pro 210 is the compact, inexpensive choice. On an M4 or newer Air, the Plugable Thunderbolt dock drives two monitors natively with no driver.

On an M1 to M3 Air with the lid open, two monitors need DisplayLink: the PULWTOP is the budget option, the TobenONE 18-in-2 the fuller dock with 2.5G Ethernet, and the WAVLINK the choice for 5K monitors. The Anker DL6350 is the only route to three.
